questions.question: A line passing through the point $\mathrm{P}(\sqrt{5}, \sqrt{5})$ intersects the ellipse $\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{36}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{25}=1$ at $A$ and $B$ such that $(P A) .(P B)$ is maximum. Then $5\left(P A^2+P B^2\right)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation: Given ellipse is $\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{y^2}{25}=1$ Any point on line $A B$ can be assumed as $\mathrm{Q}(\sqrt{5}+\mathrm{r} \cos \theta, \sqrt{5}+\mathrm{r} \sin \theta)$ Putting this in equation of ellipse, we get $25(\sqrt{5}+r \cos \theta)^2+36(\sqrt{5}+r \sin \theta)^2=900$ Simplifying, we get $\begin{aligned} &$ $\mathrm{r}^2$\left(25 $\cos$ ^2 $\theta$+36 $\sin$ ^2 $\theta$\right)$+2 $\sqrt{5} \mathrm{r}$(25 $\cos \theta$+36 $\sin \theta$)-595=0 \\ & $\quad$|$\mathrm{r}$|=$\mathrm{PA}$, $\mathrm{~PB}$ \end{aligned}$ $\text { Thus, } $$\begin{aligned} \text { PA } \cdot \mathrm{PB} & =\frac{595}{25 \cos ^2 \theta+36 \sin ^2 \theta}=\frac{595}{25+11 \sin ^2 \theta} \\ & =\text { maximum, if } \sin ^2 \theta=0 \end{aligned}$$ This means line $A B$ must be parallel to $x$-axis $\Rightarrow y_A=y_B=\sqrt{5}$ Putting $\mathrm{y}=\sqrt{5}$ in equation of ellipse, we get $\frac{x^2}{36}+\frac{1}{5}=1 \Rightarrow x^2=36 \cdot \frac{4}{5}$ Hence, $\mathrm{PA}^2+\mathrm{PB}^2=\left(\sqrt{5}-\frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{5}+\frac{12}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2 \begin{aligned} & =2\left(5+\frac{144}{5}\right)=\frac{338}{5} \\ & 5\left(\mathrm{PA}^2+\mathrm{PB}^2\right)=338\end{aligned}$ ,

questions.question: Let $A(\alpha ,0)$ and $B(0,\beta )$ be the points on the line $5x + 7y = 50$. Let the point $P$ divide the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $7 : 3$. questions.explanation: Given: $A(\alpha ,0)$ and $B(0,\beta )$ lies on the line $5x + 7y = 50$. $\implies 5\left(\alpha \right) + 7\left(0\right) = 50,5\left(0\right) + 7\left(\beta \right) = 50 \implies \alpha = 10,\beta = \frac{50}{7}$ Also, $P$ divide the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $7 : 3$. $\implies P \equiv \left(\frac{7 \times 0 + 3 \times 10}{7 + 3},\frac{7 \times \frac{50}{7} + 3 \times 0}{7 + 3}\right) \implies P \equiv \left(3,5\right) \implies ae = 3$ as perpendicular from $S$ passes through $P$ Now, $3x - 25 = 0$ is a directrix of the ellipse $E : \frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1 \implies x = \frac{25}{3}$ We know that, directrix of an ellipse is given by $x = \pm \frac{a}{e} \implies \frac{a}{e} = \frac{25}{3}$ Also, $ae = 3 \implies a = 5,b = 4$ Length of LR $= \frac{2{b}^{2}}{a} = \frac{32}{5}$ !

questions.question: If the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse {x}^{2} + 4{y}^{2} + 2x + 8y - \lambda = 0$ is $4$, and $l$ is the length of its major axis, then $\lambda + l$ is equal to _____.
questions.explanation:
Given,

{x}^{2} + 4{y}^{2} + 2x + 8y - \lambda = 0$ is a ellipse

Now on rearranging the terms we get,

$\implies \frac{{\left(x + 1\right)}^{2}}{\lambda + 5} + \frac{{\left(y + 1\right)}^{2}}{\frac{\lambda + 5}{4}} = 1$

We know that length of latus rectum is $\frac{2{b}^{2}}{a} = 4$

So, $\frac{2\left(\lambda + 5\right)}{4\left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right)} = 4 \implies \frac{2\left(\lambda + 5\right)}{4} = 4\left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right) \implies \left(\lambda + 5\right) = 8\left(\sqrt{\lambda + 5}\right) \implies {\left(\lambda + 5\right)}^{2} = 64\left(\lambda + 5\right) \implies {\lambda }^{2} + 25 + 10\lambda = 64\left(\lambda + 5\right) \implies {\lambda }^{2} - 54\lambda - 295 = 0 \implies \lambda = 59\text{or } - 5$

But $\lambda \ne - 5$

So, $l = 2a = 2\sqrt{\lambda + 5} = 2\sqrt{64} = 16 \implies \lambda + l = 59 + 16 = 75$

questions.question: If the points of intersection of two distinct conics {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 4b$ and $\frac{{x}^{2}}{16} + \frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$ lie on the curve {y}^{2} = 3{x}^{2}$, then $3\sqrt{3}$ times the area of the rectangle formed by the intersection points is _______.
questions.explanation: Given conics are {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 4b\text{and}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16} + \frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$. The intersection point of these conics lie on {y}^{2} = 3{x}^{2}$. So, putting {y}^{2} = 3{x}^{2}$ in both the conics. $\implies {x}^{2} + 3{x}^{2} = 4b,\frac{{x}^{2}}{16} + \frac{3{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1 \implies {x}^{2} = b,\frac{b}{16} + \frac{3b}{{b}^{2}} = 1 \implies \frac{b}{16} + \frac{3}{b} = 1 \implies {b}^{2} + 48 = 16b \implies {b}^{2} - 16b + 48 = 0 \implies {b}^{2} - 12b - 4b + 48 = 0 \implies \left(b - 4\right)\left(b - 12\right) \implies b = 4,12$ ( $b = 4$is rejected because curves coincide) $\implies b = 12 \implies x = \pm \sqrt{12} \implies 12 + {y}^{2} = 48 \implies y = \pm 6$ Hence points of intersection are $( \pm \sqrt{12}, \pm 6)$. So, length and breadth of rectangle are $2\sqrt{12}\text{and}12$. So, the area of rectangle is given by, $A = 2\sqrt{12} \times 12 = 48\sqrt{3} \implies 3\sqrt{3}A = 48\sqrt{3} \times 3\sqrt{3} \implies 3\sqrt{3}A = 432$

questions.question: Let $\mathrm{E}_1: \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$ be an ellipse. If $A_i$ is the area of the ellipse $E_i$, then $\frac{5}{\pi}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)$, is equal to
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_1=\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{9}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4} \Rightarrow \mathrm{e}=\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ & \mathrm{E}_2: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4}=1 \\ & \mathrm{e}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}=\sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{9}=1-\frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4} \\ & \mathrm{a}^2=\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_2: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{4}=1 \\ & \mathrm{E}_3: \frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1 \\ & \mathrm{e}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}=\sqrt{1-\frac{\mathrm{b}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}} \Rightarrow b^2=\frac{64}{81}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_3=\frac{\mathrm{x}^2}{\frac{16}{9}}+\frac{\mathrm{y}^2}{\frac{64}{81}}=1 \\ & \mathrm{~A}_1=\pi \times 3 \times 2 \Rightarrow 6 \pi \\ & \mathrm{~A}_2=\pi \times \frac{4}{3} \times 2=\frac{8 \pi}{3} \\ & \mathrm{~A}_3=\pi \times \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{8}{9}=\frac{32 \pi}{81} \\ & \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}}=6 \pi+\frac{8 \pi}{3}+\frac{32 \pi}{81}+\ldots . \infty \Rightarrow \frac{6 \pi}{1-\frac{4}{9}} \Rightarrow \frac{54 \pi}{5} \\ & \therefore \frac{5}{\pi} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{\infty} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{\pi} \times \frac{54 \pi}{5}=54\end{aligned}$

Since, the ellipse {E}_{2}$ touches the major axis of the ellipse {E}_{1}$, hence, the minor axis of the ellipse {E}_{2}$ is {a}_{1} = a.$ Now, let the major axis of the ellipse {E}_{2}$ is {b}_{1} = c$ and it is obvious from the diagram and the given conditions that {b}_{1} > {a}_{1}.$ We know that the eccentricity of an ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{{A}^{2}} + \frac{{y}^{2}}{{B}^{2}} = 1,A > B$ is $\sqrt{1 - \frac{{B}^{2}}{{A}^{2}}}.$ Thus, for the ellipse {E}_{1},$ we have $e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}}$ and for the ellipse {E}_{2},$ we have {e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{{a}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}}.$ Given, $e = {e}_{1} \sqrt{1 - \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{{a}^{2}}{{c}^{2}}} \implies 1 - \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = 1 - \frac{{a}^{2}}{{c}^{2}} \implies \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = \frac{{a}^{2}}{{c}^{2}} \implies {c}^{2} = \frac{{a}^{4}}{{b}^{2}} \implies c = \frac{{a}^{2}}{b}...\left(i\right)$ Also, given that the foci of {E}_{2}$ are the end points of the minor axis of {E}_{1},$ thus $b = ce \implies c = \frac{b}{e}...\left(ii\right)$ From the above two equations, we get $\frac{b}{e} = \frac{{a}^{2}}{b} \implies e = \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}$ Now, using the definition of eccentricity, we get $e = \frac{{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = 1 - {e}^{2} \implies {e}^{2} + e - 1 = 0$ Now, applying the Sridharacharya's formula for the roots of a quadratic equation, i.e. if $a{x}^{2} + bx + c = 0,a \ne 0,$ then $x = \frac{ - b \pm \sqrt{{b}^{2} - 4ac}}{2a},$ we get $e = \frac{ - 1 \pm \sqrt{{1}^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times \left( - 1\right)}}{2 \times 1} \implies e = \frac{ - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4}}{2} \implies e = \frac{ - 1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$ But, eccentricity can never be negative, hence $e = \frac{ - 1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}.$ ,
